fig-anaphylaxis-positions.caption: Anaphylaxis positions (AAP Allergy and Anaphylaxis Emergency Plan, as on 02-03): keep them lying on their back; if they vomit or have trouble breathing, keep them lying on their side. Keep them lying down: do not stand them up or walk them.
fig-anaphylaxis-positions.alt: Two panels. Top: a person lying flat on their back on the floor, labelled usual position. Bottom: seen from above, a person lying on their side with the knees bent forward and the mouth pointing down, labelled if vomiting or having trouble breathing. Below, a red bar: keep them lying down, do not stand them up or walk them.

fig-ash-hopper.caption: The traditional ash hopper (13-09, an outline, not a procedure): a barrel with a false bottom and a spout; dry, sieved hardwood ash on top; soft water such as rainwater trickled slowly through; the liquid collected underneath is caustic lye. Goggles, gloves, ventilation; never boil it down.
fig-ash-hopper.alt: Cut-away of a barrel on blocks. Inside, a perforated false bottom holds a thick layer of hardwood ash; rainwater trickles in from a can at the top; liquid drips through the false bottom and runs out of a spout near the base into a bucket. Red warning labels: caustic, treat as lye; goggles and gloves; boiling it down spatters, this is where people get hurt.

fig-auto-injector-outer-thigh.caption: Epinephrine auto-injector: into the outer thigh, through clothing if needed, following the device's own instructions. For one common pen the label says hold it in place for 3 seconds, then massage the area for 10 seconds. Note the time.
fig-auto-injector-outer-thigh.alt: Front view of two legs from the hips to the knees. A shaded oval on the outside of the middle of the right thigh marks where the auto-injector goes; the pen is drawn pressed straight against the outer thigh from the side, through a trouser leg. Notes beside it: through clothing if needed; follow your device's own instructions; one common pen, hold 3 seconds then massage 10 seconds; note the time.

fig-backfeed-path.caption: Backfeeding: generator power pushed into an outlet flows out through the panel and meter to the pole transformer, which raises it to the street line's voltage and kills a line worker who believes the line is dead. The safe path: an inlet and a transfer switch or interlock, with the main breaker off.
fig-backfeed-path.alt: Two house cutaways with the service wires, the meter, the panel, a pole transformer and a line worker on the next pole. Top, crossed out: a generator outside with a cord that has two male ends pushed into a wall outlet; red arrows run from the outlet to the panel, out through the meter and the service wires to the transformer and along the street line to the worker. Bottom, ticked: the generator cord goes to an outdoor inlet and a transfer switch or interlock; the main breaker is off and nothing reaches the street.

fig-banked-fire.caption: Banking a fire (06-02): let it burn down to a good bed of coals, rake the coals into a compact pile, put one or two large, dense logs on top, and cover the edges with ash. In the morning, rake the ash off, add fine kindling and blow gently.
fig-banked-fire.alt: Side section of a fire bed: a compact mound of glowing coals in the middle, two large dense logs lying on top of it, and a layer of grey ash drawn over the edges of the mound, labelled ash insulates and slows it to a smoulder.

fig-box-fan-filter.caption: The clean room in wildfire smoke: windows and door shut, a portable air cleaner on its highest setting, or, if you have none, a box fan with a furnace filter taped to it (a temporary substitute EPA describes). No smoke made inside.
fig-box-fan-filter.alt: Plan of a closed room with its window and door shut. In the middle, a box fan seen from the side with a furnace filter taped flat against one face; arrows show room air passing through the filter and then the fan. Crossed-out icons: candle, frying pan, aerosol spray. A note: a portable air cleaner sized for the room, that makes no ozone, is better.

fig-bucket-toilet.caption: Bucket toilet: two 5-gallon buckets (one in use, one being emptied), a snap-on seat with lid, a bag liner, cover material and a scoop beside it, a separate urine jug, and handwashing right next to it.
fig-bucket-toilet.alt: Side by side: a 5-gallon bucket with a snap-on toilet seat and lid and a bag liner, labelled in use; a second bucket labelled spare, being emptied and cleaned; a bin of cover material such as sawdust with a scoop; a jug for urine; and a handwashing station with soap.

fig-burn-palm-rule.caption: The palm rule: the burned person's own palm is about 1% of their body surface (palm and fingers together about 0.8 to 1%). Count with their palm, not yours: an adult's palm on a toddler gives the wrong answer. Count blistered or worse skin; redness alone does not count.
fig-burn-palm-rule.alt: Left: an open hand, palm up, with the palm and fingers shaded and the label: their own palm, about 1 percent of their body. Right: a large adult hand beside a small toddler hand, with the adult hand crossed out for measuring a toddler: use the burned person's own palm. Below: count blistered or worse, not redness; an adult with about 10 of their own palms or more of blistered burn needs care; any child's burn bigger than a few of their own palms is serious.

fig-cal-hypo-two-step.caption: Pool shock (calcium hypochlorite), the EPA two-step method: 1, one heaping teaspoon (about 1/4 oz) of granules into 2 gallons of water makes the stock, labelled DO NOT DRINK; 2, one part stock to 100 parts water (1 pint per 12.5 gallons), stir, wait 30 minutes, expect a slight chlorine smell.
fig-cal-hypo-two-step.alt: Step 1: a heaping teaspoon of granules going into a 2-gallon bucket of water, the bucket labelled CHLORINE STOCK: DO NOT DRINK. Step 2: a pint of stock poured into 12.5 gallons of water, with the equivalents per gallon and per 5 gallons, a 30-minute clock, and a check for a slight chlorine smell. A label panel shows 65 to 73 percent calcium hypochlorite with no algaecides, clarifiers or stabilizers.

fig-candling-an-egg.caption: Candling an egg (04-15): in a dark room, hold the egg against a bright flashlight. A sound egg shows a small air pocket at the wide end and a faint yolk shadow. A large air pocket, a dark or moving mass, blotches, cracks, or a bad smell on opening: throw it out. Crack every egg into a separate bowl first.
fig-candling-an-egg.alt: Left: a hand-held flashlight shining up into an egg in a dark room. Middle: a sound egg lit from behind, with a small air pocket at the wide end and a faint yolk shadow, marked keep. Right: a bad egg with a large air pocket and a dark mass and blotches, marked throw out.

fig-chainsaw-kickback-zone.caption: Chainsaw kickback (16-06): when the upper tip of the bar touches wood or anything else, or the wood pinches the chain, the bar is thrown up and back toward you in a fraction of a second. Never let the nose of the bar touch anything; both hands on the saw, left on the front handle, right on the rear.
fig-chainsaw-kickback-zone.alt: Side view of a chainsaw. The upper quarter of the rounded bar tip is shaded red and labelled kickback zone. A curved red arrow shows the bar flying up and back toward the operator's position. The front and rear handles are labelled left hand and right hand.

fig-choking-child-adult.caption: Choking, age 1 to adult: bend them forward and give five back blows between the shoulder blades, then five abdominal thrusts from behind, fist just above the navel, in and up. Kneel behind a small child. Pregnant or too big to reach round: chest thrusts.
fig-choking-child-adult.alt: Three panels. Left: a standing person bent forward at the waist, a rescuer beside them supporting the chest with one arm and striking between the shoulder blades with the heel of the other hand, marked 5 back blows. Middle: the rescuer standing behind with arms around, a fist just above the navel, arrow in and up, marked 5 abdominal thrusts. Right: the rescuer kneeling behind a small child doing the same.

fig-choking-infant.caption: Choking infant under 1: five firm back blows with the baby face-down along your forearm, head lower than chest, jaw supported; then turn face-up for five chest thrusts with the heel of one hand on the middle of the breastbone, just below the nipples. Never abdominal thrusts under 1.
fig-choking-infant.alt: Two panels. Left: a seated adult rests a forearm on the thigh with the infant lying face-down along it, head lower than the chest and the jaw held in the hand; the palm of the other hand strikes between the shoulder blades, marked 5 back blows. Right: the infant face-up along the forearm, head lower, with the heel of one hand on the middle of the breastbone just below the nipples, marked 5 chest thrusts.

fig-chopping-block-height.caption: Chopping block height (16-06): for splitting, a low block, knee height or less, so the head arrives near the bottom of its swing with the handle about level and a miss hits the block or the ground. A waist-high splitting block sends a glancing blow forward and down into your legs. The higher block is only for hatchet and kindling work.
fig-chopping-block-height.alt: Three side-view panels. Left, ticked: a person splitting on a block at knee height or less, the maul handle about level at impact, a miss going into the block or the ground. Middle, crossed out: the same swing on a waist-high block, with a red arrow showing a glancing blow travelling forward and down into the legs. Right: a higher block used only for a hatchet splitting kindling, hands clear.

fig-closure-strips.caption: Closure strips are only for the narrow case: a clean, fresh, well-flushed, shallow cut with straight edges that meet without pulling. Lay the strips across the cut with gaps between them. Most wounds (dirty, punctures, bites, hours old, deep, crushed, over a joint) stay open: pack loosely and dress. Unsure? Leave it open.
fig-closure-strips.alt: Two panels. Top, marked with a green tick: a straight shallow cut on the skin closed with five thin strips laid across it, gaps between the strips, the edges meeting without pulling. Bottom, marked leave open: a ragged wound with loose gauze packing in it and a dressing beside it, and a list of wounds never to close: dirty, puncture, bite, more than several hours old, infected, deep, crushed, over a joint, face hands or genitals.

fig-co-alarm-placement.caption: Carbon monoxide alarms: one on every level and one outside each sleeping area; in the warm room, on the wall opposite the heater at pillow height. Never above the heater, in a ceiling corner, beside a window, door, vent or fan, or in a bathroom.
fig-co-alarm-placement.alt: Cutaway of a two-storey house with a basement. Green alarms: in the upstairs hall outside the bedrooms, on the main floor, in the basement, and in the warm room on the wall opposite the heater at the height of a sleeping person's head. Red crossed-out alarms: directly above the heater, in the corner where wall meets ceiling, beside the cracked window, and in the bathroom.

fig-coal-heat-zones.caption: Heat zones (07-01): let the fire burn down to a glowing bed of coals, then rake them into a hot zone (deep coals) for searing and boiling, a medium zone (thinner coals) for most cooking, and a cool zone (few or no coals) to move food to when it is getting ahead of you. Move the food, not the fire.
fig-coal-heat-zones.alt: Top view of a ring of stones around a fire pit with a grate across it. The coals are raked into three zones: on the left a deep pile marked hot, searing and boiling; in the middle a thinner layer marked medium, most cooking; on the right a few scattered coals marked cool, move food here. A pot and a pan sit on the grate.

fig-cord-and-plug-conversion.caption: Cord-and-plug conversion (DC-07): the furnace gets its own plug. Normal: it plugs into the receptacle where its old house circuit now ends. Outage: main breaker off and locked, furnace unplugged from the wall and plugged into the generator cord, which has one male and one female end.
fig-cord-and-plug-conversion.alt: Two rows. Normal: the panel with breakers on feeds a wall receptacle; the furnace cord and plug are plugged into it; plug and receptacle are labelled. Outage: the main breaker is off with a lock; the wall receptacle is empty; the furnace plug goes into the female end of an extension cord whose male end is in the generator outdoors. A red note says never a cord with two male ends and never into house wiring.

fig-cord-measure.caption: A full cord is 128 cubic feet: a stack 4 ft high, 4 ft deep and 8 ft long. A face cord (rick) is one row 4 ft high and 8 ft long but only 16 to 24 inches deep: a third to a half of a cord, and often sold as a "cord" (MU Extension).
fig-cord-measure.alt: Two woodpiles drawn the same height and length. The top one is a full cord, 4 feet high, 8 feet long and 4 feet deep, labelled 128 cubic feet. The bottom one is a face cord, the same 4 by 8 feet face but only 16 to 24 inches deep, labelled a third to a half of a cord.

fig-cord-tie-and-cut.caption: The cord can wait: WHO recommends clamping late, about 1 to 3 minutes after birth. When it has stopped pulsing, tie it tightly with clean (boiled) string in two places a few finger-widths apart and cut between the ties with a boiled blade. Never pull on the cord.
fig-cord-tie-and-cut.alt: A length of umbilical cord running from the baby's side on the left to the mother's side on the right. Two tight string ties sit a few finger-widths apart, and a blade cuts between them. Labels: wait 1 to 3 minutes, until it stops pulsing; boiled string; boiled blade; never pull on the cord.

fig-cpr-adult.caption: Adult CPR: heel of one hand on the centre of the chest, other hand on top, fingers interlaced, arms straight, shoulders over the hands. Push about 2 inches (5 cm) deep, 100 to 120 a minute, let the chest come fully back up. 30 compressions to 2 breaths.
fig-cpr-adult.alt: Side view of a person lying on their back on the floor and a rescuer kneeling beside them, arms straight, shoulders directly above two stacked hands on the centre of the chest. An arrow shows the push of about 2 inches. An inset shows the heel of one hand on the chest with the other hand on top, fingers laced and lifted.

fig-cpr-child.caption: Child CPR (1 year to puberty): heel of one hand on the centre of the chest, other hand on top, about 2 inches (5 cm) deep, 100 to 120 a minute. Head tilt and chin lift for breaths. 30:2 with one rescuer, 15:2 with two.
fig-cpr-child.alt: Side view of a child lying on their back and a kneeling rescuer pressing with the heel of one hand, other hand on top, on the centre of the chest, arms straight. An arrow shows a push of about 2 inches. A second small drawing shows the head tilted back with two fingers lifting the chin.

fig-cpr-infant.caption: Infant CPR (under 1 year): two thumbs side by side on the centre of the chest just below the nipple line, hands wrapped round the chest; or the heel of one hand if you cannot press deep enough. About 1½ inches (4 cm) deep, 100 to 120 a minute. No two-finger compressions. Cover mouth and nose with your mouth.
fig-cpr-infant.alt: Left: an infant on its back on a firm surface, head in a neutral sniffing position, with the heel of one hand pressing the breastbone just below the nipples and an arrow showing about 1½ inches. Right: seen from above, two hands wrap around the infant's chest with both thumbs side by side on the breastbone, the first choice.

fig-creosote-stages.caption: Creosote, as sweeps grade it (CSIA, as on 06-09): stage 1, light, flaky, sooty dust that an ordinary brush takes off; stage 2, crusty, tar-like flakes a brush struggles with; stage 3, glaze, hard, shiny or tacky black, like poured tar that set, which brushing will not remove. All of it is highly combustible. Never reach stage 3.
fig-creosote-stages.alt: Three square swatches of flue wall. Stage 1: a light grey dusting of loose soot flakes, labelled brush takes it off. Stage 2: darker, crusty, curled tar-like flakes, labelled brush struggles. Stage 3: a smooth, shiny black glaze with highlights, labelled glaze, brushing will not remove it, stop using the flue.

fig-cup-on-lid-still.caption: Cup-on-lid still (CDC): pot half full of filtered water, lid upside down, cup tied to the lid handle so it hangs upright and does not touch the water. Boil 20 minutes; the water in the cup is distilled.
fig-cup-on-lid-still.alt: Cutaway of a pot on a flame, half full of water. The lid sits upside down so its handle points into the pot; a cup is tied to the handle and hangs upright above the water. Steam rises, condenses on the lid, runs to the low middle point and drips into the cup.

fig-defensible-space-zones.caption: Defensible space (USFA, as on 17-05): 0 to 5 feet, nothing that burns (no mulch, dead plants, leaves, needles, firewood or stored items against the walls); 5 to 30 feet, lean, clean and green; woodpiles at least 30 feet from the house; 30 to 100 feet, fuel reduced by thinning, spacing and limbing up. The house: clean gutters, screened vents, nothing under or on decks, propane cylinders moved away.
fig-defensible-space-zones.alt: Plan view of a house in the middle of three rings: 0 to 5 feet shaded grey, gravel or bare soil; 5 to 30 feet with spaced, watered plants; 30 to 100 feet with thinned, spaced trees. A woodpile sits beyond the 30-foot ring. Callouts on the house: clean gutters, screened vents, nothing under the deck, propane moved away.

fig-device-fallback-ladder.caption: The pump and sensor fallback ladder (02-02): six rungs from full automation down to fast-acting insulin only. Each step down trades convenience for reliability. Never jump further down than the failure forces; never stay above a step that has stopped working. Rungs 4 and 5 need no electricity.
fig-device-fallback-ladder.alt: A ladder of six rungs, top to bottom: 1 full automation, needs pump, sensor, controller, power; 2 backup controller or reader, needs the spare already set up; 3 pump without automation, needs settings copy and sugar readings; 4 injections with a sensor, needs long- and fast-acting insulin and the prescriber's plan; 5 injections with a fingerstick meter, needs meter, strips, lancets, night alarm; 6 fast-acting insulin only, a bridge on a prescriber's plan. Rungs 4 and 5 are bracketed: no electricity needed.

fig-drilled-well-parts.caption: A drilled well (03-10): the sanitary well cap on the casing; the submersible pump hanging near the bottom on its drop pipe; the pitless adapter, where the water line leaves the casing below the frost line; the pressure tank and pressure switch in the house. A purpose-made well bucket (cylinder bailer) is slim enough to go down the casing; an ordinary bucket is not.
fig-drilled-well-parts.alt: Cut-away of the ground with a well casing going down from a capped top to water-bearing rock. Inside, a drop pipe hangs from the top to a submersible pump near the bottom, with its electric cable. Below a dashed frost line, a pitless adapter joins the drop pipe to a buried water line that runs sideways to a house wall, where a pressure tank and pressure switch stand. Beside the casing at the top, a slim well bucket on a rope, next to a crossed-out ordinary bucket.

fig-drying-rack-over-stove.caption: Drying with heat you already have (04-06): a screen rack above a wood stove, with a thermometer at rack level, is good for plant food, and for meat only if the thermometer at the rack reads 140 °F the whole time. A covered solar-drying screen is for fruit, vegetables and herbs only: never meat.
fig-drying-rack-over-stove.alt: Two panels. Left: a wood stove with a screen rack hung above it holding sliced fruit, and a thermometer clipped at rack level; label: meat only if the rack reads 140 °F the whole time. Right: a screen in the sun on blocks, covered with a fine cloth, holding fruit and herbs, with air moving under it; a crossed-out piece of meat says never meat.

fig-ducted-heater-window-board.caption: Ducted diesel heater window board: a snug board in the window with two holes, combustion intake and exhaust, both opening outdoors; the warm-air duct stays entirely indoors. Every exhaust joint sealed; the exhaust slopes slightly down and away and ends away from any window, door or vent. Battery CO alarm in the heated room, every run.
fig-ducted-heater-window-board.alt: Cross-section of a wall with a window. A board fills the bottom of the window opening, with the window closed down onto it. Inside, the heater sits on the floor; a warm-air duct leaves it and stays inside the room. Two pipes pass through the board: the combustion intake and the exhaust, which slopes slightly downward outside and ends away from the window. Labels: seal every exhaust joint, very hot, keep off siding and combustibles. A CO alarm is drawn on the room wall.

fig-dutch-oven-coals.caption: Dutch oven coals (Missouri Department of Conservation, as on 07-04): total briquettes = 2 × the diameter in inches for about 325 °F; a 12-inch oven takes 24, with two-thirds (16) on the lid and one-third (8) underneath for baking. Add or remove 2 briquettes for about 25 °F. Every 15 minutes, turn the oven a quarter turn and the lid a quarter turn the other way. Check with a thermometer.
fig-dutch-oven-coals.alt: Side view of a three-legged camp Dutch oven with a rimmed lid. Sixteen briquettes sit on the lid in a ring and eight sit underneath between the legs. Labels: 12-inch oven, about 325 °F, 24 briquettes, 16 on the lid, 8 underneath; add or remove 2 for about 25 °F. A top view shows curved arrows: oven a quarter turn one way, lid a quarter turn the other way, every 15 minutes.

fig-evaporative-pouch.caption: Evaporative cooling pouch: soak for exactly the time your instructions give, drain and towel until only semi-dry, put the medicine in, and keep it open to the air. Water evaporating through the fabric carries heat away; anything that stops evaporation (a zip bag, an airtight box) stops the cooling. It is not a refrigerator.
fig-evaporative-pouch.alt: Four small panels: a pouch soaking in a bowl of cold water beside a timer; the pouch being patted with a towel; an insulin pen going into the pouch; the pouch clipped open to the air on a belt with wavy lines leaving it. Below, crossed out in red: the pouch sealed in a zip bag, and the pouch in an airtight box.

fig-extinguisher-pass.caption: Using an extinguisher, PASS (USFA, as on 29-12): Pull the pin, nozzle pointing away from you; Aim low, at the base of the fire; Squeeze the lever slowly and evenly; Sweep side to side across the base until it is out. Only with your back to a clear exit. Label "1A:10B:C": 1A matches 1.25 gallons of water on a class A fire; 10B covers a liquid fire of about 10 square feet; C is for plugged-in electrical equipment.
fig-extinguisher-pass.alt: Four panels: P, a hand pulling the pin from the handle; A, the hose aimed low at the base of the flames; S, a hand squeezing the lever; S, the hose sweeping side to side across the base of the fire. Below, a sample label reading 1A:10B:C with each part explained, and a note: back to a clear exit; if it is not out when the extinguisher is empty, leave.

fig-fallout-decay-7-10.caption: The 7-10 rule (HHS REMM): fallout radiation falls about tenfold for every sevenfold increase in time. 1 hour: the starting level; 7 hours: about 1/10; 2 days: about 1/100; 2 weeks: about 1/1,000.
fig-fallout-decay-7-10.alt: Four bars on a logarithmic scale. 1 hour after the explosion, a full bar labelled the starting level; 7 hours, a bar one step lower labelled about 1/10; 2 days (49 hours), another step lower, about 1/100; 2 weeks, the lowest, about 1/1,000.

fig-first-flush-diverter.caption: Rain barrel set-up (03-05): the first rain off the roof carries the most dirt, germs and chemicals, so send it away from the barrel and collect what comes after. Screen and lid on the barrel, level solid base, draw from a spigot above the sediment. Then filter, boil or disinfect, and store clean. Never mix rain into treated water.
fig-first-flush-diverter.alt: A roof edge, gutter and downspout. The downspout feeds a capped side pipe first, labelled first flush, the dirtiest runoff, kept out of the barrel; once it is full, water carries on through a screen into a lidded barrel standing on a level platform. A spigot sits above the sediment layer at the bottom. An arrow leads from the spigot to three steps: filter, boil or disinfect, store clean as treated.

fig-flat-diaper-fold.caption: Cloth diapering with a flat (13-08): a single large square of cotton folded into a pad and laid in a waterproof cover, closed with snap-style fasteners or safety pins. Flats dry fastest. Scrape solids into the toilet system first; store in a lidded dry pail until wash day.
fig-flat-diaper-fold.alt: Three steps left to right: a large square of cotton; the square folded into a long pad of several layers; the pad laid inside a waterproof cover with its tabs and a safety pin or snap fastener. Below: solids into the toilet system, then a lidded dry pail.

fig-flood-water-depths.caption: Turn Around, Don't Drown (NWS): moving water 6 inches deep knocks an adult off their feet; 12 inches carries away most cars; 2 feet carries away SUVs and trucks. No depth of flowing water across a road is safe to drive, and the road under it may be gone.
fig-flood-water-depths.alt: Three panels side by side, each with moving water shown by arrows. 6 inches: water at an adult's ankles and shins, the person falling. 12 inches: a car floating off the road. 2 feet: an SUV or pickup being carried away. Below: the road under the water may be gone; never drive or walk into moving water.

fig-flue-inspection-mirror.caption: Inspecting the flue (06-09): cold flue, damper open; from the firebox or the cleanout door, angle a mirror to see up the flue and shine a strong flashlight on it. Scrape test: drag a screwdriver along the flue wall; about 1/8 inch of sooty buildup means sweep before the next fire. Shiny, tarry glaze: stop using the flue.
fig-flue-inspection-mirror.alt: Cut-away of a cold fireplace and flue. A hand holds a mirror tilted inside the firebox below the open damper, and a flashlight beam bounces off the mirror up the flue lining. An inset shows a screwdriver dragged along the flue wall, scraping a layer marked about 1/8 inch: sweep before the next fire.

fig-four-pin-connector.caption: Trailer lights (16-11): in a common 4-pin plug, the white wire and the light housings' mounting screws carry the return (ground) path; a bad ground causes most trailer light faults. Unbolt the white wire where it meets the frame, wire-brush the frame and terminal to bright metal, bolt it back tight. Pack both plug halves with dielectric grease.
fig-four-pin-connector.alt: A flat 4-pin trailer plug with four wires leaving it; the white wire is highlighted and runs to a ring terminal bolted to the trailer frame, where a wire brush cleans the metal bright. The other three wires run to the lights. Labels: white wire, ground; bolt to bright metal; dielectric grease in both halves.

fig-four-stages-of-a-resource.caption: The four stages every supply passes through (23-04): 1 stock, a pile that only shrinks; 2 extend, ration, recover, reuse, repair, so it shrinks more slowly; 3 substitute, something else does the job, usually worse; 4 produce, you make or gather it on and on. A supply is only really solved at stage 4; a supply with no stage 4 has a deadline.
fig-four-stages-of-a-resource.alt: Four steps from left to right: a pile labelled 1 stock, only shrinks; a smaller pile shrinking slowly labelled 2 extend; a different object labelled 3 substitute, usually worse; a growing plant labelled 4 produce, on and on. A bracket under stages 2 and 3 reads buys time.

fig-fuel-can-colours.caption: US fuel can colours: red gasoline, yellow diesel, blue kerosene. Propane comes only in pressure cylinders. Trust the label, not the colour: every can is labelled with its fuel.
fig-fuel-can-colours.alt: Three portable fuel cans side by side, red labelled GASOLINE, yellow labelled DIESEL, blue labelled KEROSENE, each with a hand-written label, then a grey propane cylinder and a printed metal camp-fuel can. Below: the label, not the colour.

fig-fuel-ladder.caption: The fuel ladder (06-01): four sizes, all ready before you strike anything: tinder that catches a spark; kindling from pencil-lead to pencil thickness; small fuel from finger to wrist thickness; fuel wood, the real logs. Have three times more kindling than you think you need.
fig-fuel-ladder.alt: Four piles laid out from left to right with thickness labels: tinder (a cotton ball, bark shavings, lint); kindling, thin twigs from pencil-lead to pencil thick; small fuel, sticks from finger to wrist thick; fuel wood, split logs. Under the kindling pile, a note: three times more than you think.

fig-gas-valve-on-off.caption: Natural gas shutoff at the meter: the valve is on the pipe coming out of the ground, before the meter. Bar in line with the pipe = ON; a quarter turn with a wrench so the bar lies crosswise = OFF. Propane: close the valve under the tank's dome, clockwise.
fig-gas-valve-on-off.alt: Two drawings of a gas meter on its riser pipe. Left, ON: the flat bar on the valve body points along the pipe. Right, OFF: the bar is turned a quarter turn so it lies across the pipe, with an adjustable wrench on it and a curved arrow. Below, a propane tank with the dome lid open and the valve marked clockwise to close.

fig-generator-connection-options.caption: Five ways a generator can reach something in the house. Four are allowed with the right person doing the work; backfeeding through an outlet is never allowed.
fig-generator-connection-options.alt: Five rows, each with a generator outdoors on the left and the house wall: (a) an extension cord to one appliance, always allowed; (b) a cord to an inlet on the wall and a transfer switch beside the panel, licensed electrician; (c) a cord to an inlet and an interlock plate on the panel so the main breaker and the generator breaker are never on together, licensed electrician; (d) a furnace unplugged from its wall receptacle and plugged into the generator cord, a cord-and-plug conversion, decision card DC-07; (e) a cord with two male ends pushed into a wall outlet, crossed out in red: backfeed, never.

fig-generator-distance.caption: Where the generator runs: outdoors, 20 feet or more from any window, door or vent, exhaust pointed away from every house, never in a garage or under a deck or overhang.
fig-generator-distance.alt: Plan view from above. A house with windows, a door and a vent, an attached garage and a deck. Inside the garage and under the deck a generator is crossed out in red. Out in the yard a generator sits 20 feet or more from the nearest window, its exhaust arrow pointing away from the house and away from the neighbour's house. A checklist below repeats the rules and says to keep battery carbon monoxide alarms on inside.

fig-generator-siting.caption: Where the generator runs: outdoors, 20 feet or more from any window, door or vent, exhaust pointed away from every house, never in a garage or under a deck or overhang.
fig-generator-siting.alt: Plan view from above. A house with windows, a door and a vent, an attached garage and a deck. Inside the garage and under the deck a generator is crossed out in red. Out in the yard a generator sits 20 feet or more from the nearest window, its exhaust arrow pointing away from the house and away from the neighbour's house. A checklist below repeats the rules and says to keep battery carbon monoxide alarms on inside.

fig-haybox.caption: The haybox (07-02): bring the food to a full rolling boil right through the pot, then move the covered pot into a heavily insulated box. Check with a thermometer before serving: still above 140 °F is fine; just dropped below 140 °F, reheat to 165 °F; below 140 °F for more than 2 hours, throw it out (CDC). Dry beans: soak, discard the water and boil 30 minutes first.
fig-haybox.alt: Two steps. Left: a lidded pot on a fire at a full rolling boil, bubbles right through. Right: the same covered pot packed inside a cooler stuffed with towels, with a thermometer. A table of three outcomes: above 140 °F fine; just below 140 °F reheat to 165 °F; below 140 °F for more than 2 hours throw out.

fig-heat-index-chart.caption: NWS heat index chart: air temperature across the top, relative humidity down the side. Colours: Caution, Extreme Caution, Danger, Extreme Danger. Full sun can add up to 15 °F.
fig-heat-index-chart.alt: The National Weather Service heat index table, 80 to 110 degrees F across and 40 to 100 percent relative humidity down, coloured in four bands from Caution to Extreme Danger.
fig-heat-index-chart.credit: NOAA National Weather Service, Heat Index chart. Public domain (US Government work).

fig-heat-ladder-house-to-bag.caption: Why small is warm (08-06): as fuel gets short, step down to smaller spaces with the same heat source, you: house, one room, a tent inside the room, sleeping bags inside the tent, layers inside the bags.
fig-heat-ladder-house-to-bag.alt: Five nested outlines, each inside the last: a house, one room inside it, a tent inside the room, a sleeping bag inside the tent, and a person in layers inside the bag. Each is labelled, with an arrow showing the steps from house to layers.

fig-heater-barrier-clearances.caption: A fixed, anchored barrier around the heater at the clearances on its label, the hot-zone line taped on the floor, the play area on the far side from the heater and its air openings, and the CO alarm at pillow height.
fig-heater-barrier-clearances.alt: Plan view of a room. The heater stands inside a ring of play-yard panels anchored to the wall, set back by the clearances printed on its label, with blanks to write the above, front and side distances. A taped line on the floor marks the hot zone that children do not cross. The play area and crib are on the far side of the room from the heater and the air openings. The CO alarm is on the far wall at pillow height.

fig-ice-thickness.caption: New clear ice (Minnesota DNR, as on 05-08): under 4 inches, stay off; 4 inches, walking and ice fishing on foot; 5 to 7 inches, snowmobile or small ATV; 7 to 8 inches, side-by-side ATV; 9 to 10 inches, small car or SUV; 11 to 12 inches, medium SUV or small truck; 13 inches, medium truck. White ice is about half as strong: double every figure. No ice is ever "safe" ice.
fig-ice-thickness.alt: A stacked bar chart of clear-ice thickness from under 4 inches to 13 inches, each band labelled with the load it carries: stay off; on foot; snowmobile or small ATV; side-by-side ATV; small car or SUV; medium SUV or small truck; medium truck. A note: white ice, double every figure.

fig-inhaler-with-spacer.caption: Rescue inhaler with a spacer: sit upright, leaning slightly forward; the inhaler fits into the back of the spacer and the mouthpiece goes in the mouth. How many puffs, and when, comes from the person's written action plan, not from this picture.
fig-inhaler-with-spacer.alt: Left: a person sitting upright on a chair, leaning slightly forward, holding a tube-shaped spacer to the mouth with the inhaler fitted into its far end. Right: a close-up of the spacer: the inhaler canister in its plastic boot pushed into the back end, the tube, and the mouthpiece at the front. A box below says the number of puffs comes from the written action plan.

fig-insulin-cooler-barrier.caption: Ice or cold packs with a barrier: a towel or a box between the ice and the insulin so it cannot freeze, and a min/max thermometer beside the insulin. Aim for the label's 36 to 46 °F and never let it freeze: frozen insulin is discarded.
fig-insulin-cooler-barrier.alt: Cut-away of an insulated cooler. Cold packs stand against both sides and lie on the bottom. A folded towel lines the space between the packs and a small box in the middle, which holds the insulin. A min/max thermometer probe sits beside the insulin box, its display outside the lid. A red label: insulin never touches ice. Notes: aim for 36 to 46 °F; never let it freeze; frozen insulin is discarded.

fig-jar-headspace-and-seal.caption: Canning jar: headspace is the empty space between the food and the lid, set by the recipe. Sealed: the lid is pulled down (concave) and does not flex. Unsealed: fridge and eat now, or reprocess with a new lid. Bulging lid: throw away without tasting.
fig-jar-headspace-and-seal.alt: Left: cross-section of a canning jar with band and flat lid, the food level, and the headspace between food and lid marked as the recipe says. Right, three lids side by side: sealed, dipped in the centre, ticked; unsealed, flexing up and down when pressed, marked fridge and eat now or reprocess; bulging, domed up, crossed out and marked throw away, do not taste.

fig-kerosene-flame-height.caption: Wick kerosene heater flame, seen through the glass: correct is a ½-inch flame above the flame spreader, even all round. Too high gives smoke and soot (lower the wick); too low gives smell and carbon monoxide (never run below the wick stop). Check at 5 to 7 minutes, then every 30 minutes.
fig-kerosene-flame-height.alt: Three side-by-side drawings of a heater burner seen through its glass. Left, marked correct: an even flame about half an inch above the flame spreader. Middle, too high: tall uneven flames with smoke and soot above. Right, too low: a flame barely above the wick, marked smell and carbon monoxide.

fig-knot-bowline.caption: Bowline in four steps: the small loop, the working end up through it, around behind the standing part, back down the loop, tightened. The tail finishes inside the big loop.
fig-knot-bowline.alt: Four photographs of a rope on a table: 1, a small loop made in the standing part with the working end lying beside it; 2, the working end passed up through the small loop; 3, the end taken around behind the standing part; 4, the finished bowline with a fixed loop.
fig-knot-bowline.credit: US Air Force, AFH 10-644, Survival Evasion Resistance Escape (SERE) Operations, 27 March 2017, Figure 15-31 (printed page 257). Photo by SSgt Justin Watters, USAF. Public domain (US Government work).

fig-knot-clove-hitch.caption: Clove hitch. Top row: tied in the hand as two loops laid one over the other and dropped over a post or clip. Bottom row: tied around a pole, two wraps side by side with the crossing pinned between them.
fig-knot-clove-hitch.alt: Six photographs. Top: two loops in a rope, the loops overlapped, then dropped over a carabiner and pulled snug. Bottom: a rope wrapped around a green pole, crossed over itself, and tucked under the second wrap to form a clove hitch.
fig-knot-clove-hitch.credit: US Air Force, AFH 10-644, Survival Evasion Resistance Escape (SERE) Operations, 27 March 2017, Figure 15-36 (printed page 261). Photo by SSgt Justin Watters, USAF. Public domain (US Government work).

fig-knot-overhand.caption: Overhand knot: a loop, the working end pushed through from behind, both ends pulled.
fig-knot-overhand.alt: Photograph of a red and black rope tied in a single overhand knot on a wooden table.
fig-knot-overhand.credit: US Air Force, AFH 10-644, Survival Evasion Resistance Escape (SERE) Operations, 27 March 2017, Figure 15-25 (printed page 253). Photo by SSgt Justin Watters, USAF. Public domain (US Government work).

fig-knot-parts-of-a-rope.caption: The words used in every knot step: working end, standing part, bight, loop.
fig-knot-parts-of-a-rope.alt: One rope drawn across the frame. The short free end on the right is labelled working end; the long rest on the left is labelled standing part. Below, a U-shaped fold with no crossing is labelled bight, and a circle where the rope crosses itself is labelled loop.

fig-knot-prusik.caption: Prusik: a closed loop of thinner cord wrapped three times around a thicker rope. It slides when you push the wraps and grips when the loop is pulled. Not for holding a person.
fig-knot-prusik.alt: A thick horizontal ridge line. A closed loop of thin cord is passed around it three times, each wrap inside the last, so three neat turns sit side by side; the loop hangs down below with an arrow showing the pull that makes it grip.

fig-knot-round-turn-two-half-hitches.caption: Round turn and two half hitches: two turns around the pole, then two half hitches around the standing part, slid down against the pole.
fig-knot-round-turn-two-half-hitches.alt: Three photographs of a rope tied to a green pole: the round turn, the first half hitch around the standing part, and the finished knot with two half hitches.
fig-knot-round-turn-two-half-hitches.credit: US Air Force, AFH 10-644, Survival Evasion Resistance Escape (SERE) Operations, 27 March 2017, Figure 15-37 (printed page 261). Photo by SSgt Justin Watters, USAF. Public domain (US Government work).

fig-knot-sheet-bend.caption: Sheet bend: a bight in the thicker rope, the thin end up through it, around behind both legs, tucked under itself. Both short ends finish on the same side.
fig-knot-sheet-bend.alt: Three photographs: a white thick rope folded into a U with a thinner red rope coming up through it, the red rope wrapped behind the U, and the finished sheet bend.
fig-knot-sheet-bend.credit: US Air Force, AFH 10-644, Survival Evasion Resistance Escape (SERE) Operations, 27 March 2017, Figure 15-29 (printed page 256). Photo by SSgt Justin Watters, USAF. Public domain (US Government work).

fig-knot-square-knot.caption: Square knot: right over left, then left over right; each rope's two strands leave the knot on the same side and it lies flat. Below, crossed out: the granny knot, which slips.
fig-knot-square-knot.alt: Top: three photographs of a red rope and a blue rope tied into a square knot step by step. Bottom: two photographs of a granny knot, crossed out in red with the words granny knot slips, untie and start again.
fig-knot-square-knot.credit: US Air Force, AFH 10-644, Survival Evasion Resistance Escape (SERE) Operations, 27 March 2017, Figure 15-27 and 15-28 (granny knot panels) (printed page 255). Photo by SSgt Justin Watters, USAF. Public domain (US Government work). Titles and red cross added by GoettschePreppy.

fig-knot-taut-line-hitch.caption: Taut-line hitch on a guy line: around the anchor, then two wraps around the standing part inside the loop, one wrap outside it, tucked. It slides by hand and holds under load.
fig-knot-taut-line-hitch.alt: A stake at the left and a tarp at the right. The line runs from the tarp to the stake, around it and back toward the tarp. The working end makes wraps 1 and 2 around the standing part inside the big loop, then wrap 3 on the tarp side outside the loop, and is tucked under that last wrap. Arrows show the knot sliding along the standing part to tighten.

fig-knot-truckers-hitch.caption: Trucker's hitch: far end tied off, a pulley loop in the standing part, the working end around the anchor and back up through the loop, pulled tight, locked with two half hitches.
fig-knot-truckers-hitch.alt: Side view of a load on a trailer bed. The rope is tied to a fixed point on the far side, runs over the load and down toward the anchor hook. About two feet above the anchor a hanging loop is formed in the standing part. The working end goes down around the anchor, back up through the loop, and is pulled down; two half hitches lock it around both strands below the loop.

fig-lashing-diagonal.caption: Diagonal lashing: a clove hitch around both poles where they cross (some guides use a timber hitch), three turns along one diagonal, three along the other, frapping turns, clove hitch to finish.
fig-lashing-diagonal.alt: Three photographs of a cord lashing two crossed poles: the starting hitch and first diagonal wraps, the wraps on the other diagonal, and the finished lashing with frapping turns.
fig-lashing-diagonal.credit: US Air Force, AFH 10-644, Survival Evasion Resistance Escape (SERE) Operations, 27 March 2017, Figure 15-41 (printed page 264). Photo by SSgt Justin Watters, USAF. Public domain (US Government work).

fig-lashing-square.caption: Square lashing: clove hitch on the upright, three or four wraps around the joint, frapping turns between the poles, clove hitch to finish.
fig-lashing-square.alt: Four photographs of a cord lashing a horizontal yellow pole across an upright wooden pole: the starting hitch, the wraps, the frapping turns, and the finished lashing.
fig-lashing-square.credit: US Air Force, AFH 10-644, Survival Evasion Resistance Escape (SERE) Operations, 27 March 2017, Figure 15-40 (printed page 263). Photo by SSgt Justin Watters, USAF. Public domain (US Government work).

fig-latrine-setbacks.caption: Latrine siting: downhill of the well and at least 100 ft from it and from any surface water, 50 ft or more from the house, never in a drainage path or floodplain; at least 5 ft of dry soil under the bottom of the pit.
fig-latrine-setbacks.alt: Top, plan view on a slope with an arrow pointing downhill. The well is uphill; the house is between; the latrine is downhill, at least 100 ft from the well and at least 100 ft from a creek, and 50 ft or more from the house. Bottom, side view of the pit with at least 5 ft of dry soil between its bottom and the water table.

fig-layer-system.caption: The layer system (11-01): base layer against the skin moves sweat away (wool or synthetic, never cotton); mid layer traps air, which is the warmth (fleece, wool, down, synthetic fill); outer shell blocks wind and water; extremities, head, hands, feet and face, are where frostbite happens. Several thin layers beat one thick one.
fig-layer-system.alt: A cut-away of layers over skin, from the inside out: base, a thin band with sweat arrows moving outward, never cotton; mid, a thick band of trapped air dots, the warmth; outer shell, a thin band with wind and rain arrows bouncing off. Beside it, small icons of a hat, gloves, boots and face cover labelled extremities.

fig-lug-star-pattern.caption: Lug nuts go on in a star pattern, across the wheel, not round the circle (16-10): hand-tight in a star, lower the vehicle, tighten firmly in the star, then torque to the owner's manual at the first chance and recheck after a short drive.
fig-lug-star-pattern.alt: Two wheels seen face-on. A five-lug wheel with the nuts numbered 1 to 5 in a star order, each number across from the last, joined by a star-shaped line. A six-lug wheel numbered 1 to 6 in a criss-cross order, each nut followed by the one opposite.

fig-mc4-polarity-check.caption: Check a panel string before plugging it in: meter on DC volts, red probe to the + lead, black to the − lead. A minus sign on the display means a connector is reversed: swap it.
fig-mc4-polarity-check.alt: A multimeter set to DC volts with its red probe touching the panel lead marked plus and its black probe on the minus lead. One display shows a plain number labelled correct; a second display shows the same number with a minus sign, labelled reversed, swap it before anything is plugged in.

fig-micron-scale-germs.caption: Germ sizes against filter pore sizes (29-06): parasites such as Giardia and Cryptosporidium are removed by a filter of 1 micron or finer; bacteria by 0.3 micron or finer; viruses are far smaller, and most portable filters do not remove them, so filtered water still needs chlorine or boiling unless the box says viruses.
fig-micron-scale-germs.alt: A horizontal scale in microns, with each step ten times the last, from 0.01 to 100. Bars show viruses at the small end, bacteria around one micron, and Giardia and Cryptosporidium larger. Vertical lines mark filter pore sizes of 0.3 and 1 micron; parasites are to the right of both, bacteria are to the right of 0.3, and viruses are to the left of both, labelled most portable filters do not stop these.

fig-mylar-bucket-pack.caption: The container system (04-03): a food-grade bucket, a Mylar liner bag, dry food (about 10 percent moisture or less), oxygen absorbers sized to the container and opened last, the Mylar sealed with a clothes iron or hair straightener, then the lid, and a label on the outside: contents, weight, date packed and the ingredient label.
fig-mylar-bucket-pack.alt: Cut-away of a 5-gallon bucket. Inside, a Mylar bag full of dry grain with oxygen absorbers on top; the top of the bag is folded over and sealed with a hot iron. A lid sits above. A label on the outside lists contents, weight, date packed and ingredients. A small jar beside it holds the unused absorbers, resealed at once.

fig-naloxone-nasal-spray.caption: Naloxone nasal spray (Narcan 4 mg Drug Facts, as on 02-17): thumb on the bottom of the plunger, nozzle into either nostril, press firmly; each device sprays once. Not awake after 2 to 3 minutes: another dose with a new device, and keep going every 2 to 3 minutes until they wake. Then on their side; not breathing normally, start CPR. Stay with them.
fig-naloxone-nasal-spray.alt: A person lying on their back, seen from the side, with the head tipped slightly back. A hand holds a nasal spray device with the nozzle in one nostril and the thumb on the bottom of the plunger. A box to the right reads: no wake-up in 2 to 3 minutes, next dose with a new device, either nostril, keep going until they wake. Below, numbered steps: spray, call 911, watch and repeat, on their side or CPR, stay.

fig-newborn-skin-to-skin.caption: Dry the baby at once with a clean cloth and lay it skin to skin on the mother's bare chest, both covered, the baby's head covered. A wet baby loses heat fast.
fig-newborn-skin-to-skin.alt: A mother half sitting up against pillows with a newborn lying on its front on her bare chest. A blanket covers both of them up to the baby's shoulders, and the baby wears a cap. Labels: dried at once, skin to skin, both covered, head covered.

fig-oxygen-no-flame-zone.caption: Medical oxygen: at least 5 feet between the oxygen and any heat source, open flame or electrical device; never a candle, match, lighter, oil lamp or wood stove near it; no smoking by anyone, with No Smoking and No Open Flames signs. Best: a room with no flame at all.
fig-oxygen-no-flame-zone.alt: Room plan. In the middle, a chair with an oxygen concentrator beside it and a dashed circle around them marked at least 5 feet. Inside the circle, nothing. Outside the circle, crossed out for inside it: a candle, an oil lamp, a space heater, a gas stove and a wood stove, which is in a different room. A No Smoking and No Open Flames sign is on the door. Notes: no aerosol sprays, vapour rub, petroleum jelly or oil-based lotions; turn the oxygen off when not in use.

fig-panel-transfer-switch-interlock.caption: Backfeeding: generator power pushed into an outlet flows out through the panel and meter to the pole transformer, which raises it to the street line's voltage and kills a line worker who believes the line is dead. The safe path: an inlet and a transfer switch or interlock, with the main breaker off.
fig-panel-transfer-switch-interlock.alt: Two house cutaways with the service wires, the meter, the panel, a pole transformer and a line worker on the next pole. Top, crossed out: a generator outside with a cord that has two male ends pushed into a wall outlet; red arrows run from the outlet to the panel, out through the meter and the service wires to the transformer and along the street line to the worker. Bottom, ticked: the generator cord goes to an outdoor inlet and a transfer switch or interlock; the main breaker is off and nothing reaches the street.

fig-plunger-agitator.caption: Hand laundry (13-04): agitate with a plunger in a bucket (movement, not temperature, removes most dirt); wring hard and rinse once or twice; wring again, then roll the item in a dry towel and stand on it; dry on a high line in the warm room or outdoors.
fig-plunger-agitator.alt: Four panels. 1: a plunger pumped up and down in a bucket of soapy laundry. 2: hands twisting a wet item to wring it. 3: an item rolled up inside a dry towel on the floor with a foot standing on it. 4: clothes hanging on a high line.

fig-power-bank-rotation.caption: Power-bank rotation (00-10): number your power banks. At any moment one is in use, one is charging (from a power station, a solar panel, or a vehicle that is running anyway) and one is full and set aside as the reserve. Empty goes to charging; charged becomes the reserve; the reserve goes into use. Tape the number and the fill date on each.
fig-power-bank-rotation.alt: Three numbered power banks in a clockwise cycle: in use, in a pocket charging a phone; charging, from a power station, solar panel or running vehicle; full reserve, set aside, with a tape strip showing number and date. Arrows run from in use to charging to reserve and back to in use.

fig-pressure-canner-parts.caption: Pressure canner parts: weighted gauge or dial gauge, vent port (petcock), safety fuse, gasket, vent/cover lock, jar rack.
fig-pressure-canner-parts.alt: Labelled cutaway drawing of a pressure canner holding jars of green beans on a rack, with the weighted gauge, dial gauge, one-piece safety counterweight, vent port, safety fuse, gasket and vent and cover lock called out.
fig-pressure-canner-parts.credit: USDA National Institute of Food and Agriculture, Complete Guide to Home Canning (2015 revision), Guide 1: Principles of Home Canning, page 1-19. Public domain (US Government work).

fig-pressure-points.caption: Where pressure sores form (MedlinePlus): where bone presses skin against a mattress or seat: back of the head, shoulder blades, elbows, tailbone, hips, knees, ankles, heels and ears. In bed, change position every 1 to 2 hours; in a wheelchair, shift weight every 15 to 20 minutes. Pillows between knees and ankles, under the calves to lift the heels; none under the knees; no donut cushions.
fig-pressure-points.alt: Three outlines. Lying on the back: red dots on the back of the head, shoulder blades, elbow, tailbone and heels, with a pillow under the calves so the heels float. Lying on the side: red dots on the ear, shoulder, hip, knee and ankle, with a pillow between the knees and ankles. Sitting in a wheelchair: red dots on the tailbone and shoulder blades, with the note shift weight every 15 to 20 minutes.

fig-propane-heater-hose-route.caption: Portable propane heater on a 20-lb tank: the tank outdoors on a board, the maker's hose through a cracked ground-level window or door with a towel at the gap, the fuel filter at the heater's regulator, both air openings open, and the CO alarm on the opposite wall at pillow height.
fig-propane-heater-hose-route.alt: Cutaway of a room at ground level and the yard outside. Outside, a 20-lb propane tank stands upright on a board. The maker's hose runs from the tank valve through a window cracked at ground level, with a towel round the gap, to the heater on the floor inside. The fuel filter sits between the hose and the heater regulator. The heater has its clearances marked, 30 inches above, 24 inches in front, 6 inches each side. A 3 by 3 inch opening at ceiling level and another at floor level are open. The CO alarm is on the far wall at pillow height.

fig-propane-pools-low.caption: How an indoor propane cylinder hurts people (30-03): a slow leak overnight spreads along the floor, where nobody smells it at standing height; the heater, lit in the morning, or a water-heater pilot across the room catches the edge of the cloud and it burns all at once.
fig-propane-pools-low.alt: Cut-away of a room. A propane cylinder stands beside a heater; a shaded layer of gas flows from a loose connection along the floor across the room, under a standing person whose nose is well above it, to a water heater with a pilot flame at floor level. Labels: slow leak overnight, spreads along the floor, nobody smells it at standing height, pilot or heater lights the edge of the cloud.

fig-recovery-position.caption: Recovery position: on their side, top knee bent forward to stop them rolling, head tilted back and mouth pointing down so vomit drains and the airway stays open. Check breathing.
fig-recovery-position.alt: Seen from above, a person lying on their side. The lower arm is out in front, the upper hand is under the cheek, the head is tilted back with the mouth pointing toward the ground, and the upper leg is bent forward at hip and knee so the knee rests on the ground in front of the body.

fig-rocket-stove-cutaway.caption: Rocket stove (07-02): an insulated L-shaped burn chamber; fuel feeds in sideways on a shelf while air passes underneath; the short vertical chimney makes a strong draft; the pot sits on supports with a gap so the hot gases reach it. Level, non-combustible ground; never indoors, in a tent or in a garage.
fig-rocket-stove-cutaway.alt: Cut-away of an L-shaped rocket stove. Sticks lie on a shelf in the horizontal feed tube, with an air arrow passing under the shelf. The burn chamber turns upward into a short vertical chimney surrounded by insulation such as wood ash or vermiculite inside an outer can. A pot sits on small supports above the chimney top, with a gap for the hot gases to flow out around the pot.

fig-sawbuck.caption: A sawbuck (16-06): an X-shaped stand that holds wood at working height while sawing. Build one; it prevents many injuries.
fig-sawbuck.alt: Side view of a sawbuck: two X-shaped leg frames joined by a rail, with a log lying in the upper V of the crosses at about hip height. A bow saw cuts the log between the two frames, and a person stands upright beside it.

fig-septic-system.caption: How a septic system works (EPA, as on 13-12): waste water runs down one main drain into a buried, watertight tank; solids sink as sludge, fats and grease float as scum, and the cleared liquid in the middle (effluent) flows out to the drain field, shallow covered trenches in dry soil, where the soil does the treatment.
fig-septic-system.alt: Cut-away of the ground beside a house. A main drain pipe slopes from the house into a buried tank showing three layers: scum floating at the top, clear effluent in the middle and sludge on the bottom. Tank lids or risers show at the surface. An outlet pipe leads to a drain field of shallow covered trenches with perforated pipes, and arrows show the liquid soaking down through the soil, which treats it before it reaches groundwater.

fig-series-vs-parallel.caption: Series adds voltage, parallel adds current. Do the cold-voltage check before any series string, and never put a series string into a station with a low input-voltage ceiling.
fig-series-vs-parallel.alt: Top: three panels of about 20 V wired plus to minus in a chain make about 60 V. A box says add the label Voc of every panel, multiply by 1.20, and the result must be below the station maximum PV input voltage. A station with a high voltage ceiling is ticked; a station with a low ceiling is crossed out. Bottom: two panels joined plus to plus and minus to minus with Y-branch connectors make about 20 V with the currents added.

fig-signal-mirror-aiming.caption: Aiming a signal mirror (US Air Force survival handbook): put one hand out in front of the mirror at arm's length and form a "V" with two fingers; with the target in the V, tilt the mirror so most of the reflected light passes through the V. Needs sun and practice.
fig-signal-mirror-aiming.alt: Three photographs of service members aiming signal mirrors. Left: a man holds a small mirror near his eye and stretches his other arm out with two fingers raised in a V. Middle: a close-up of a mirror with a sighting hole held against the face below the eye. Right: a man in gloves sighting through a mirror with his other hand raised.
fig-signal-mirror-aiming.credit: US Air Force, AFH 10-644, Survival Evasion Resistance Escape (SERE) Operations, 27 March 2017, Figure 21-5, Aiming Signal Mirror (printed page 502). Public domain (US Government work).

fig-solar-box-cooker.caption: Box solar cooker (07-03): a cardboard box inside a larger box, the gap packed with crumpled newspaper or wool; the inside lined with aluminium foil; a dark pot with a lid inside; a clear plastic or glass lid; foil-covered flaps as reflectors. An oven thermometer inside; do not open it to look.
fig-solar-box-cooker.alt: Cut-away of two nested cardboard boxes with crumpled paper insulation in the gap. The inner box is lined with foil and holds a dark lidded pot and an oven thermometer. A clear lid covers the top, and a foil-covered reflector flap is propped up behind, bouncing sunlight down through the clear lid.

fig-splint-joint-above-below.caption: Splinting: splint it as you found it, holding still the joint above and the joint below the break, with padding in every gap. Leave fingers and toes showing so you can check colour, warmth, pulse, feeling and wiggle before and after; if they get worse, loosen it at once. A broken finger can be taped to its neighbour.
fig-splint-joint-above-below.alt: Three drawings. Forearm: a rigid splint runs from the palm past the elbow, padding fills the gaps, three ties hold it, and the fingertips are left showing; the elbow and wrist are labelled joint above and joint below. Lower leg: splints on both sides run from above the knee to past the foot, padded, tied in several places, toes showing; knee and ankle labelled. Finger: the injured finger taped to the finger beside it with two bands of tape and padding between them. Below: check before and after, loosen at once if worse, re-check often.

fig-splitting-stance.caption: Splitting safely (06-03): chopping block at about knee height, never on the ground; feet apart and out of the swing line, so a glancing blade hits the block or the dirt, not your shin; nobody near you while you split, especially children.
fig-splitting-stance.alt: Side view of a person splitting a round on a knee-high chopping block. The feet are apart and back from the block; the maul's arc is drawn ending in the round and, if it glances, in the block and the ground, never the shin. A dashed circle around the scene is labelled keep everyone well clear.

fig-sprouting-jar.caption: Sprouting in a jar (04-16): soak the seed overnight, drain completely, then rinse and drain twice a day, morning and evening, with the jar tilted mouth-down so it drains, at room temperature, out of direct sun. Ready in 2 to 6 days, when the sprout is about as long as the seed. Musty, sour, slimy or mouldy: throw it out.
fig-sprouting-jar.alt: A glass jar with a mesh lid tilted mouth-down in a bowl so water drains out. Beside it, a row of four seeds showing the stages: soaked seed, a seed just splitting, a short sprout, and a sprout about as long as the seed marked ready.

fig-stroke-fast.caption: Stroke, F.A.S.T. (American Stroke Association): Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call 911 and note when it started. Any one sign means act. If the person has diabetes and a meter is at hand, check blood sugar first: a low can look exactly like a stroke. No aspirin for a possible stroke.
fig-stroke-fast.alt: An amber bar across the top reads: diabetes and a meter or sensor, check blood sugar first, a low looks like a stroke. Below it, four tiles. F: a face with one side of the mouth drooping, ask for a smile. A: a person with both arms raised and one drifting down. S: a speech bubble with jumbled words, slurred or wrong words. T: a clock, note the time it started and go. At the bottom: any one sign means act; no aspirin for a possible stroke.

fig-three-classes-of-consumable.caption: Three classes of supply (23-01): A, renewable, you can make or gather more (water, wood, garden food): build the ability to produce it. B, substitutable, it runs out but something else does the job (batteries to daylight, gauze to boiled cloth): stock deeply and learn the substitute. C, irreplaceable, no way to make it and nothing replaces it (prescription medicines the body depends on): class C is short, and it decides everything.
fig-three-classes-of-consumable.alt: Three columns. A, renewable, in green, with examples water, wood, garden food, soap and the plan: build the ability to produce it. B, substitutable, in amber, with examples batteries to daylight, gauze to boiled cloth, tape to wire, and the plan: stock deeply and learn the substitute. C, irreplaceable, in red, with examples insulin, epinephrine, seizure and heart medicines, and the line: class C is short, and it decides everything.

fig-three-phases.caption: The binder's spine: A, shelter in place at home for as long as home works; the go or no-go decision; B, movement; C, establish at a destination or wherever you end up. You can turn back from B to A, and move again from C.
fig-three-phases.alt: Three boxes left to right, A shelter in place, B movement, C establish. Between A and B a diamond reads go or no-go. A curved arrow from B back to A is labelled turn back; a curved arrow from C back to B is labelled move again.

fig-three-tub-dishwashing.caption: Three-tub dishwashing (13-10): scrape first; tub 1 WASH, hot water and soap, cleanest to dirtiest; tub 2 RINSE, clean warm water; tub 3 SANITIZE, 1 tablespoon of unscented 5 to 9 percent bleach in 1 gallon of clean water, dishes fully under; then air dry on a rack, no towel. The sanitize tub is not drinkable. Wash and rinse water become greywater.
fig-three-tub-dishwashing.alt: A row of steps from left to right: a plate being scraped into a waste bin; three tubs labelled 1 wash, hot water and soap; 2 rinse, clean warm water; 3 sanitize, 1 tablespoon bleach per gallon, dishes fully under, not drinkable; then a drying rack labelled air dry, no towel. Arrows from tubs 1 and 2 to a greywater bucket.

fig-tippy-tap.caption: Tippy-tap (13-02): a jug hung from a frame with a small hole near the cap, tipped by a string tied to a foot pedal; soap hangs on a string beside it. Hands-free and uses very little water. Built from a jug, cord, two sticks and a nail.
fig-tippy-tap.alt: Two upright sticks with a crossbar. A jug hangs from the crossbar by its handle; a string runs from the jug's cap down to a stick lying on the ground as a foot pedal. A foot presses the pedal and the jug tips, pouring a thin stream from a small hole near the cap onto hands. A bar of soap hangs on a string from the crossbar. The rinse water runs off and away from the station.

fig-tornado-vehicle-choices.caption: Tornado while in a vehicle (NWS, SPC, as on 17-02): a sturdy building always wins. If the tornado is far off and roads are open, drive at right angles to its path. Caught by extreme wind or debris: park out of traffic lanes, stay in with the seat belt on, head below the windows, covered. Leave the car only for ground noticeably lower than the road. Never shelter under an overpass.
fig-tornado-vehicle-choices.alt: Four panels. 1: a map view with a tornado track and a car turning to drive away at a right angle to it. 2: a car parked off the lane, the driver belted with head down below the windows, covered by a coat. 3: a person lying flat in a ditch that is noticeably lower than the road, head covered. 4: a car stopped under an overpass, crossed out in red.

fig-tourniquet-placement.caption: Tourniquet: 2 to 3 inches above the wound, on the limb, never over a joint. Tighten until the bleeding stops and there is no pulse below, lock the windlass, write the time on it, never loosen it. Still bleeding: a second tourniquet above the first.
fig-tourniquet-placement.alt: Two legs drawn lying flat. Top: a wound on the thigh; a windlass tourniquet sits 2 to 3 inches above it, between the wound and the body, with the windlass rod locked in its clip and TIME written on the strap; a dashed second tourniquet is shown above the first for when bleeding continues. Bottom: a wound just below the knee; a tourniquet over the knee is crossed out in red, and the correct one is above the knee on the thigh.

fig-tsunami-natural-warnings.caption: Tsunami natural warnings (NWS, as on 17-15): a strong or long earthquake; the ocean suddenly rising like a fast flood or a wall of water, or draining away; a loud roar from the ocean. Any one means go now, to high ground or as far inland as you can. Do not wait for an official warning. The first wave may not be the last or the largest.
fig-tsunami-natural-warnings.alt: Three icons in a row: a shaking ground line labelled strong or long earthquake; a shoreline with the sea drawn rising or draining away; an ear with a roar from the ocean. A large arrow points from all three up a hill to high ground, labelled go now.

fig-tube-condenser-still.caption: Tube-condenser still (03-03): pot half full of pre-filtered water at a low rolling boil, lid sealed around 10 to 20 ft of soft copper tube that slopes downhill the whole way through a bucket of cold water or snow to the collection jar. Never vinyl or PVC tube; never let the pot boil dry; throw away the salty liquid left in the pot.
fig-tube-condenser-still.alt: A pot on a fire with its lid sealed around a copper tube. The tube leaves the lid, coils downward through a bucket of cold water and snow, and comes out near the bottom to drip into a jar. Arrows show steam going up the tube and water dripping into the jar. Labels: half full, low rolling boil; sealed lid; copper coil slopes downhill all the way; keep the bath cold; never boil dry.

fig-two-bin-humanure.caption: Two-bin composting (13-06): bin one receives, every addition covered at once with a thick layer of straw, leaves or sawdust; when it is full it rests, closed and undisturbed for as long as you can possibly manage, while bin two receives. Then swap. Bins closed on all sides, rodent- and child-proof, on soil, placed by 13-07.
fig-two-bin-humanure.alt: Two closed bins side by side on soil, each with a lid and hardware-cloth sides. The left bin is labelled 1, receiving: waste covered at once with a thick carbon layer. The right is labelled 2, resting: lid closed, undisturbed as long as possible. A curved arrow says swap when bin 1 is full. Notes: on soil, downhill and far from water, the edible garden and the kitchen.

fig-vapour-flow.caption: Gasoline vapour is heavier than air: it flows along the floor and can be lit by a water heater's pilot light across the room (Maryland Department of the Environment). Never pour or transfer fuel inside the garage.
fig-vapour-flow.alt: Cut-away of an attached garage. A gasoline can sits at one side; a shaded layer of vapour flows from it along the floor, past a car, to a gas water heater with a pilot flame at floor level on the far wall. The shared wall and door to the house are on the right. Labels: vapour is heavier than air, flows along the floor; pilot light across the room.

fig-vehicle-recovery-setup.caption: Pulling a stuck vehicle: a rated strap with no metal hooks, attached to rated recovery points or the hitch receiver with a rated shackle, never the hitch ball; a blanket or mat over the middle of the strap; everyone else farther away than the strap is long and out of line with the pull.
fig-vehicle-recovery-setup.alt: Two vehicles nose to tail, seen from the side and from above. A recovery strap runs between them from the receiver of the pulling vehicle, through a shackle, to a rated recovery point on the stuck one; a hitch ball is crossed out. A blanket hangs over the middle of the strap. From above, a shaded no-standing zone covers the line of pull and extends past both vehicles; people stand to the side, farther away than the strap is long.

fig-warm-room-layout.caption: The warm room: heater behind a barrier at its label clearances, the heater's air openings, the door closed and hung with a blanket, everyone sleeping in the room, the CO alarm on the wall opposite the heater at pillow height.
fig-warm-room-layout.alt: Plan view of one room. The heater stands near the outside wall with the window, inside a barrier drawn at the clearances on its label. The door is closed with a blanket hung over it. Mattresses and a small tent are at the far side, pillows toward the wall opposite the heater, where the CO alarm is mounted at pillow height. An inset shows the window wall from inside: a 3 by 3 inch opening at ceiling level and another at floor level for a propane heater, or the window cracked at least 1 inch for a wick kerosene heater when the room is smaller than its manual requires.

fig-water-cascade.caption: Cascade your water (13-03): clean water, then rinsing, then washing, then dishwater, then flushing or non-food plants. Each drop is used two or three times. Greywater is used the same day, poured on the soil, never on anything eaten raw.
fig-water-cascade.alt: Five basins stepping down from left to right like stairs, joined by arrows: clean water, rinse, wash, dishwater, and at the bottom a toilet bowl and a non-food plant. Notes under them: greywater the same day, on the soil not the leaves, never for drinking, cooking, food or hands.

fig-water-heater-valves.caption: Getting water out of a tank water heater: heat off (gas control to OFF, or the breaker off), close the cold-water inlet valve on top, open a hot tap higher in the house, then open the drain valve at the base slowly into a hose or bucket. The water can be scalding.
fig-water-heater-valves.alt: A tank water heater seen from the front. On top, the cold-water inlet pipe with its valve, marked close, and the hot outlet pipe. Low on the front, the gas control knob marked OFF, not pilot, or for an electric heater the breaker off. At the base, the drain valve with a hose running to a bucket, marked open slowly, scalding. A note shows a hot tap upstairs left open to let air in. Numbers 1 to 4 follow the draining steps.

fig-watts-and-watt-hours.caption: The four words as water in a hose (29-02): volts are pressure, amps are how much water flows, watts are pressure × flow (watts = volts × amps), and watt-hours are the water in the bucket (watt-hours = watts × hours). A 1,000 Wh battery runs a 100 W load for roughly 10 hours, less losses.
fig-watts-and-watt-hours.alt: A tap feeds a hose that fills a bucket. Labels: volts, the pressure pushing; amps, how much water flows; watts, pressure times flow, how fast it is being used; watt-hours, the water collected in the bucket. Below, a worked example: 1,000 watt-hours divided by 100 watts is about 10 hours, less losses.

fig-wind-chill-chart.caption: NWS wind chill chart: find the air temperature across the top and the wind speed down the side. Shaded bands show frostbite in 30, 10 and 5 minutes.
fig-wind-chill-chart.alt: The National Weather Service wind chill table, temperatures 40 to minus 45 degrees F across, wind 5 to 60 mph down, with wind chill values in each cell and three shaded frostbite-time bands, plus the wind chill formula.
fig-wind-chill-chart.credit: NOAA National Weather Service, Wind Chill Chart (effective 1 November 2001). Public domain (US Government work).

fig-wood-year-lag.caption: The wood calendar (24-03): fell and cut to length in late winter to early spring; split in spring; stack off the ground, covered on top and open on the sides, through summer; move a winter's worth close to the house in autumn; in winter, burn last year's wood. Wood cut this year is next year's fuel.
fig-wood-year-lag.alt: A year drawn as a wheel of five steps: late winter to early spring, fell and cut; spring, split; summer, stack and dry; autumn, move near the house; winter, burn last year's wood. A separate arrow leaves the cut step and jumps a full turn ahead to next winter, labelled this year's wood burns next winter.

fig-wound-packing.caption: Wound packing for the groin, armpit or neck, where a tourniquet cannot go: push gauze in until the wound is full, then press hard on top and keep pressing. Never pack the chest or belly: cover and press.
fig-wound-packing.alt: Left: a simple body outline. The groin, armpit and neck are marked in green as places to pack; the chest and belly are shaded red with "do not pack: cover and press". Right, two cross-sections of a wound below the skin: first, fingers push a long strip of gauze into the wound until it is filled; second, two hands stacked on top press straight down hard.
